analysis.one_liner: Bans grocery stores from price gouging and from using surveillance data or electronic shelf labels to set prices.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to two House committees in August 2025 with 93 Democratic cosponsors, and neither committee has taken any action since.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would make it a federal offense, enforced by the FTC, for a grocery store to charge a 'grossly excessive price' unless it can show the price reflects real cost increases. It would also ban stores from setting a shopper's price based on personal data collected through surveillance — including facial recognition — and would require physical stores larger than 10,000 square feet to scrap electronic shelf labels in favor of paper tags. Consumers could sue violators for at least $3,000 per violation, triple damages for knowing violations, and would keep the right to sue despite pre-dispute arbitration clauses.
analysis.who_benefits: Everyone who buys groceries, but especially lower-income households, who spend the largest share of their income on food and have the least ability to absorb sudden price spikes or personalized 'surveillance pricing' charged to them based on their data profile. Shoppers also gain clear signage of prices on paper tags and notice when a store uses facial recognition.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits a retail food store from selling an item at a grossly excessive price, with an affirmative defense only if the price increase is directly attributable to costs outside the store's control; the FTC would define the term, considering a benchmark of 120% or more of the item's average price over the prior six months.

Prohibits stores from adjusting an item's price for a consumer based on the consumer's personal information — including data gathered through facial recognition — or from using electronic shelf labels to change a price based on personal data.
Bans stores larger than 10,000 square feet from using electronic shelf labels or any digital shelf display, requiring non-digital price tags instead.
Requires stores using facial recognition technology to post clear signage at the main entrance disclosing the use and its purpose.

Gives the FTC enforcement power under the FTC Act, lets state attorneys general sue on behalf of residents for actual damages or $3,000 per violation, and creates a private right of action for consumers with triple damages for willful violations, attorney's fees, and an override of pre-dispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers for these claims.
Authorizes $5 million in appropriations to carry out the Act, available through fiscal year 2032.

analysis.who_pays: Large grocery chains, which would face FTC and private enforcement over pricing, would be barred from surveillance-based pricing, and would have to replace electronic shelf labels with paper tags in big stores — plus the retail technology vendors that sell those labels and facial recognition systems. Online grocery sellers pay nothing: the bill explicitly excludes online entities.
analysis.who_pays_short: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors

drawbacks.text: The bill exempts online entities from its definition of retail food store, so online grocery sellers could continue personalized and rapidly changing pricing that physical stores are barred from — a loophole that gives e-commerce an advantage over brick-and-mortar grocers.

The ban on electronic shelf labels applies even though the technology can also be used to quickly lower prices or display unit-price comparisons, and stores that already invested in the displays would bear replacement costs; critics of price-gouging rules more broadly also argue that capping prices during shortages can worsen shortages by removing the price signal that brings in more supply.

The bill leaves the central definition — what counts as a 'grossly excessive price' and a 'market' — to future FTC rulemaking rather than fixing it in statute, so the practical reach of the gouging ban would depend on how the Commission writes the rules.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For grocery shoppers the upside is direct: prices on the shelf are what everyone pays, price spikes during shortages face a federal check, and stores cannot quietly charge different shoppers different amounts based on their data. The main real weaknesses are the online-seller carve-out, which undercuts the bill's purpose as grocery moves online, and compliance costs for large chains that have already rolled out digital shelf labels. On balance the consumer protections outweigh those costs, but the carve-out is a serious gap an honest supporter would acknowledge.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Energy and Commerce and Judiciary committees, and neither committee has held a hearing, marked it up, or sent it to the floor.

narrative.text: Rep. Rashida Tlaib (D-MI) introduced the Stop Price Gouging in Grocery Stores Act of 2025 on August 12, 2025, joined by 23 other original cosponsors.
The bill was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and, in addition, to the House Judiciary Committee on the day of introduction.
The bill has 93 cosponsors, all Democrats, with no Republican support.
The full action history shows no further action after the committee referrals — no hearings, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large grocery chains and the vendors selling them electronic shelf labels and facial recognition systems are better off for now, since the restrictions would not take effect; online grocery sellers also keep a pricing freedom the bill would have denied their physical competitors.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Large grocery chains and retail tech vendors

sides.party_line_note: All 93 cosponsors are Democrats and there is no Republican support on record; with Republicans chairing both committees of referral, the bill has not moved past its introduction-day referrals.

industries.note: The bill bars them from grossly excessive pricing, personalized surveillance-based pricing, and electronic shelf labels in stores over 10,000 square feet, and exposes them to FTC, state, and private lawsuits. Their interest in blocking it runs against shoppers' interest in stable, uniform shelf prices.

industries.industry: Electronic shelf label and retail display technology vendors
industries.note: A ban on digital shelf displays in large physical stores would cut off their core grocery market, and the technology's main commercial use — instantly changing prices per shopper or per hour — is precisely what the bill targets.

industries.industry: Facial recognition and consumer data analytics firms
industries.note: The bill bans pricing shoppers by personal or biometric data collected in stores and requires disclosure where facial recognition is used, closing off grocery retail as a data-collection and personalized-pricing market.

The bill expressly excludes online entities, so e-commerce grocers keep the freedom to personalize and dynamically adjust prices that their brick-and-mortar competitors would lose — a relative advantage won at the expense of uniform protection for shoppers.

analysis.trajectory: With no committee action in the months since referral, no Republican cosponsors, and divided control of the House, the bill is very unlikely to get a hearing or markup; the typical path for a bill at this stage with one-party support is to sit in committee until the Congress ends.
